title: Mitigating Convergence Collapse in Fixed-Target Anomaly Detectors via Kernel-Anchored Locality Regularization

paper.title: Mitigating Convergence Collapse in Fixed-Target Anomaly Detectors via Kernel-Anchored Locality Regularization
paper.abstract: Abstract. A family of tabular anomaly detectors trains a neural map toward a fixed target under squared-error loss and scores anomalies by the test-time residual; contraction matching, one-step rectified flow, and reconstruction autoencoders all fit this template. We characterize a convergence collapse : better optimization makes the detector worse. At convergence, the learned map tracks the target even off-distribution, so the residual signal vanishes on anomalies as well as on normal data. These detectors therefore rely on implicit non-convergence (early stopping, capacity caps) to retain signal. We argue this is structural: effective anomaly detection requires a locality constraint that blocks unconstrained extrapolation. Classical detectors ( k k NN, KDE, isolation forests, LOF) enforce locality explicitly; fixed-target neural detectors do not. We formalize the connection by showing that the kernel-regression analog of a fixed-target detector is a finite-bandwidth Nadaraya–Watson smoother, which we call Kernel Contraction Matching (KCM). KCM is closed-form, training-free, and CPU-efficient, yet matches established neural baselines on ADBench. Building on this bridge, we introduce the Kernel-Anchored Regularizer (KAR), which penalizes deviation of the neural prediction from a kernel-weighted average of training targets. Across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three backbones, KAR mitigates collapse and improves AUROC under prolonged training.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: A four-panel figure showing that fixed-target anomaly detectors improve early in training and then collapse as training continues; the anomaly scores flatten, and the AUROC drops while the training loss keeps decreasing. Figure 1. Convergence collapse across fixed-target anomaly detectors. Top: the anomaly-score field flattens along training, until the anomalies (stars) are no longer separated from the normal cluster (dots). Bottom left: on ADBench ( Han et al., 2022 ) 7_Cardiotocography , the methods reach an early peak ( ⋆ \star ) and then decay toward convergence ( ▽ \triangledown ). A four-panel figure showing that fixed-target anomaly detectors improve early in training and then collapse as training continues; the anomaly scores flatten, and the AUROC drops while the training loss keeps decreasing. Tabular anomaly detection identifies records that depart from normal behaviour, a long-standing problem with stakes in fraud screening, intrusion detection, condition monitoring, and medical diagnosis ( Han et al., 2022 ; Bouman et al., 2024 ) . A growing number of detectors share one design, the fixed-target template: a neural network is trained on normal data to map every input to a predetermined target , a value set in advance as a function of the input alone, and a test point is scored by its residual , the distance between the network’s output and that target. The reconstruction autoencoder uses the input itself as its target ( Sattarov et al., 2025 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ) ; flow-matching detectors instead regress a velocity field ( Li et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025a ) , with contraction matching aiming that velocity at a fixed point. Fitting a fixed target is ordinary squared-error regression, with no adversarial game, no density model, and no anomaly labels; the score is the residual, read off in one forward pass. This approach carries an implicit promise. Trained by regression, the detector should only get sharper with more epochs and a lower training loss, so training to convergence looks like good practice. We find the opposite. As the squared-error loss is minimized, detection quality first improves and then degrades. The failure is intrinsic to this class of methods, and we call it convergence collapse . At the optimum the network reproduces the fixed target on the normal data; because the target is a fixed function and the network is free to extrapolate, it reproduces the target off the normal distribution too, exactly where anomalies lie. The residual then shrinks on anomalies just as it shrinks on normal points, and AUROC declines even as the loss keeps falling. The collapsed detector is not mistrained: it has correctly solved its squared-error problem, and that problem was not detection. The pattern is not specific to one backbone: it has been studied for reconstruction autoencoders, where an expressive network reconstructs anomalies as accurately as normal points ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Ghafourian et al., 2025 ) , and we show the same failure across contraction matching and flow matching. Figure 1 shows an autoencoder, a contraction matching detector (TCCM ( Li et al., 2025a ) ), and a flow-matching detector (REFLECT ( Beizaee et al., 2025 ) ), each climbing to an early peak and then decaying toward convergence. The published strength of fixed-target detectors therefore rests on implicit non-convergence : early stopping and capacity caps that are tuned, rarely reported, and increasingly automated without naming the failure they prevent ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . The root cause is a missing constraint. The squared-error loss constrains the network only on the training data, so its score at a test point can be set by free extrapolation rather than by the nearby training points. The methods that dominate tabular benchmarks ( Han et al., 2022 ; Bouman et al., 2024 ) , among them k k -nearest-neighbour distance, the local outlier factor ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , kernel density estimation, one-class SVM ( Schölkopf et al., 1999 ) , and isolation forest ( Liu et al., 2008 ) , rest on the opposite discipline: the score at a point is set mostly by training points in a bounded neighbourhood of it. We call this property locality . Classical detectors enforce it by construction; a fixed-target neural detector, left to converge, does not. Convergence collapse is the absence of a locality constraint. Locality also points to a cure. 1 1 1 Code, configurations, and run logs: https://github.com/jose-melo/kernel-contraction-matching . Consider the kernel-regression analog of a fixed-target detector, the smoother a wide network approaches in its lazy training regime ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) . For the contraction target we call this analog Kernel Contraction Matching ( kcm ): instead of learning a map, it predicts a kernel-weighted average of the training targets, in which each training point’s influence decays smoothly with distance. kcm has no optimizer and no epoch axis, and runs on a CPU. Even so, on ADBench it matches established neural baselines ( Han et al., 2022 ; Ruff et al., 2018 ) , in line with the finding that non-deep methods are hard to beat on tabular data ( Grinsztajn et al., 2022 ) . And kcm cannot collapse: every training point’s influence is local, so its prediction levels off as a test point leaves the data and the residual grows on far anomalies instead of vanishing. kcm shows a collapse-proof solution exists, but does not let a practitioner keep a neural backbone, so we turn it into a regularizer. The Kernel-Anchored Regularizer ( kar ) penalizes the deviation of the neural prediction from the kcm prediction across the input domain, confining the network to a narrow tube around the collapse-immune kcm solution. The tube width is the only knob, expressed directly in the units of the data, so there is no loss weight to tune. Within the tube the anomaly score stays close to the kcm score at every input, AUROC can move only slightly, and the collapsed constant solution falls outside the hypothesis class. Across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three backbones, kar mitigates collapse and improves AUROC under prolonged training. The division of labour between the two is plain: kcm is the detector to deploy when scoring is the whole task; kar is for when a trainable backbone is a requirement rather than a choice , because the pipeline fine-tunes the map downstream, needs a differentiable score, or must expose a learned representation. kar ’s benchmark-wide contribution is the removal of the collapse at no accuracy cost against its anchor, not an accuracy gain over kcm . We make three contributions: (1) Convergence collapse: we show that fixed-target detectors degrade as they converge, because the network matches its target off the normal distribution and the residual vanishes on anomalies; the guarantee is formal for backbones whose training covers the off-data region and empirical for the clean-input ones (§ 3.2 ). We give a taxonomy of anomaly detectors by their off-data score behaviour. (2) Kernel Contraction Matching: we identify the kernel analog of any fixed-target detector as a closed-form, training-free, collapse-immune smoother that still matches established neural baselines on ADBench. (3) Kernel-Anchored Regularizer: we anchor a neural backbone to kcm and show this removes the collapse across all 47 47 ADBench datasets and three backbones at no accuracy cost against the anchor; on the collapse-prone subset it also improves on it.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: Anomaly detection spans a long line of method families ( Chandola et al., 2009 ) , and its deep-learning branch is by now broad ( Pang et al., 2021 ) . Most deep detectors for tabular data learn a model of normal data and score a test point by how poorly that model accounts for it: reconstruction autoencoders by the reconstruction error ( Sattarov et al., 2025 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ) , one-class networks such as Deep SVDD by the distance to a compact centre ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) , self-supervised detectors by the consistency of a pretext prediction ( Shenkar and Wolf, 2022 ; Qiu et al., 2021 ; Yin et al., 2024 ; Thimonier et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) . A more recent line scores the residual of a generative model: diffusion-based detectors read off a denoising signal ( Livernoche et al., 2024 ; Dai et al., 2025 ) , and flow-matching detectors regress a velocity field toward a fixed target, first for images ( Li et al., 2025b ; Beizaee et al., 2025 ) and then, through contraction matching, for tabular data ( Li et al., 2025a ) . All fit the fixed-target template, and we study a failure shared by the whole template rather than adding another detector to it. Classical detectors predate these deep models and remain strong baselines on tabular benchmarks ( Han et al., 2022 ; Goldstein and Uchida, 2016 ; Bouman et al., 2024 ) . Neighbourhood methods score a point from its proximity to nearby training samples: the k k -nearest-neighbour distance ( Ramaswamy et al., 2000 ) , the local outlier factor ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , and kernel density estimation ( Lang et al., 2022 ) . One-class SVMs separate the data from the origin with a kernel of bounded reach ( Schölkopf et al., 1999 ) ; isolation forests ( Liu et al., 2008 ) and the copula-based COPOD ( Li et al., 2020 ) rank a point by how extreme it is relative to the training sample as a whole. In each design the score is read from the stored training data rather than from a parametric map free to extrapolate; LUNAR ( Goodge et al., 2022 ) folds the same neighbourhood structure back into a graph neural network. That a deep detector can be harmed by additional training is already documented, along two strands. The first concerns contamination: when the unlabelled training data contains outliers, a discriminative network fits the inliers before the outliers ( Wang et al., 2019 ) , so detection peaks early and falls as the outliers are absorbed ( Nkashama et al., 2025 ) , prompting label-free stopping criteria such as EntropyStop ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and GradStop ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) alongside evaluation protocols for unstable runs ( Perini et al., 2025 ) . The second concerns reconstruction autoencoders trained on clean normal data: a sufficiently expressive autoencoder reconstructs some anomalies as accurately as normal points ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Ghafourian et al., 2025 ) , met by autoencoder-specific responses such as a memory module ( Gong et al., 2019 ) or a penalty on the latent norm ( Ghafourian et al., 2025 ) . A third failure is mode collapse in Deep SVDD, averted by architectural restrictions on bias and activations ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) or, when those restrictions prove limiting, by explicit regularizers ( Chong et al., 2020 ) . We show the effect is a property of the entire fixed-target template, following from a single missing ingredient, locality, which also yields the cure. Our treatment of that failure draws on the link between wide networks and kernel regression: in the lazy training regime the network behaves like a fixed kernel predictor governed by the neural tangent kernel ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) , a picture normally used to study generalization, and recently to build kernel predictors for tabular models directly ( Miftachov et al., 2026 ) . We use it in the opposite direction, asking which kernel smoother a fixed-target detector corresponds to, and find that this smoother retains the locality the trained network loses. Kernel density estimation already turns a kernel smoother into an anomaly score ( Lang et al., 2022 ) ; our construction applies the same principle to the contraction target rather than to the data density.

sections.heading: 3. Convergence Collapse
sections.text: Fixed-target detectors degrade as they are optimized. This section makes the assertion precise.

sections.heading: Scope of Proposition 2 .
sections.text: The collapse rests on two premises: the target T T is fixed in advance, and ℱ \mathcal{F} can realize T T on the region that matters. The support of μ \mu decides which backbones the guarantee covers. (i) Formal. Contraction matching and the rectified-flow detectors train on a noised marginal, so supp ⁡ ( μ ) \operatorname{supp}(\mu) covers the off-manifold region where anomalies lie and Proposition 2 applies with no further assumption: the optimum drives the residual to zero on anomalies as exactly as on normal points. (ii) Empirical. The reconstruction autoencoder and Deep SVDD ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) (target a constant c c ) train on the clean normal cloud, so Proposition 2 pins s ≡ 0 s\equiv 0 only there; off it the residual depends on how ℱ \mathcal{F} extrapolates the near-identity (resp. near-constant) map. For these backbones the off-manifold part of the claim is empirical, not proved: the smooth networks used in practice extrapolate their on-data fit, and Table 2 shows the same decay on both. A regularity assumption on the realized map off supp ⁡ ( μ ) \operatorname{supp}(\mu) , a Lipschitz bound on m ⋆ − T m^{\star}-T , is the hypothesis that would make case (ii) formal; we do not assume it. Figure 1 shows the collapse along training: in the lower panels, nine detectors trained on the ADBench 7_Cardiotocography dataset for 3000 3000 epochs and 3 3 seeds all reach an early AUROC peak and then degrade, although the training loss keeps decreasing. The peak-to-final AUROC drop is 0.128 0.128 for the autoencoder, 0.051 0.051 for contraction matching, and 0.017 0.017 for the rectified-flow detector. The best epoch is unstable: in Figure 1 it varies by more than two orders of magnitude and depends on the seed. The optimized loss is also misleading, since it decreases monotonically while AUROC follows an inverted-U curve, so monitoring the training loss pushes the detector toward collapse. This is not ordinary overfitting. Overfitting is a finite-sample failure, the empirical objective improving while population performance worsens; convergence collapse is a population-objective failure, the optimum itself having no anomaly signal, which Proposition 2 proves independently of train–test generalization. The experiments agree: the held-out-normal residual tracks the training residual with a median difference of 0.01 0.01 along the contraction backbone’s trajectory, far below the normal–anomaly gap the detector must preserve. Proposition 2 also names the only two ways out, one per premise. Negating the first gives a density-coupled target, the route of family T2. Negating the second restricts ℱ \mathcal{F} so that the constant target is unreachable on the region that matters; a finite-bandwidth local smoother does exactly this, the route this paper takes next.

sections.heading: Why build on a limit that excludes feature learning?
sections.text: The infinite-width theory behind Theorem 1 assumes no features are learned, while large finite networks are valued exactly because they warp their empirical tangent kernel toward the task, so a method drawn from the lazy limit can look self-contradictory. Feature learning, however, is the mechanism that lets a finite network match the fixed target off the data, and Proposition 2 says that this is what collapse is. A non-feature-learning prior is not an oversight here; it supplies the one thing the feature-learning regime cannot, an off-hull floor on the score. kar (Section 6 ) does not claim the lazy limit describes the trained network; it uses the kernel smoother as a constraint set, and its radius prices the tension: ρ = 0 \rho=0 is the anchor with no feature learning, ρ → ∞ \rho\to\infty is full feature learning and full collapse. How much feature learning survives inside the tube is not measured here; an empirical-tangent-kernel drift measurement along training would quantify it.

sections.heading: 5. KCM is Competitive on ADBench
sections.text: Section 4 introduced kcm as a closed-form detector and proved it cannot collapse. A separate question is whether a detector built to avoid a failure mode also detects anomalies well. We answer it on ADBench: kcm is level with the strongest label-free detectors on the benchmark, and it gets there with no training, no GPU, and no labels.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We follow the semi-supervised protocol. For each dataset kcm is fit on a sample of normal points and scores a held-out mixture of normal and anomalous points; the fit is the procedure of Section 4 unchanged ( β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 ), no anomaly labels enter it, and features are standardized per coordinate. We report mean AUROC over the 47 47 datasets, averaged over three seeds. kcm ’s numbers are our runs; the baseline numbers come from the TCCM benchmark ( Li et al., 2025a ) , which reports per-dataset AUROC for its 44 44 baselines plus TCCM on the same 47 47 ADBench datasets.

sections.text: ADBench ( Han et al., 2022 ) collects 47 47 tabular datasets from healthcare, finance, image-derived, and network domains, spanning nearly four orders of magnitude in sample size and up to more than a thousand features.

sections.heading: 6. Kernel-Anchored Regularization
sections.text: kcm cannot collapse, at a price: it has no trainable parameters, so a dataset cannot improve it. The vanilla fixed-target detector is trainable, and Section 3 showed that training is what destroys it. This section keeps the trainable neural map and removes the failure by constraining it to a fixed radius of the kernel-weighted average, a regularizer that is collapse-proof for the same structural reason kcm is.

sections.heading: 7. Discussion
sections.text: kcm was built to avoid convergence collapse, and Section 5 shows the construction costs nothing in accuracy: a closed-form local smoother is level with the strongest label-free detectors on the benchmark. The mean-AUROC lead over the next methods is a tie within run-to-run noise, so the substance is the asymmetry behind it: the detectors that match kcm are trained neural networks, and kcm matches them with no gradient training, no GPU, and no labels. The accuracy is stable across the benchmark, with mean AUROC about 0.88 0.88 on the low-dimensional datasets ( D ≤ 10 D\leq 10 ), 0.87 0.87 in the middle range, and 0.85 0.85 on the high-dimensional ones ( D > 50 D>50 ). The O ⁡ ( N 2 ​ D ) O(N^{2}D) fit is the main limitation; Section 5 (R3) prices it: the N 0 = 2000 N_{0}=2000 cap makes the fit constant in N N at a measured cost within ± 0.01 \pm 0.01 AUROC.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Two limitations bound the kar claim, two more the locality argument itself. kar is anchored to kcm , so where the kernel anchor is near chance it has nothing to sharpen; vertebral is that case, and kar does not help there. Across the full benchmark kar matches the anchor rather than improving on it; the benchmark-wide contribution is the removal of the collapse at no accuracy cost. The locality argument is strongest for extrapolative anomalies, points that leave the training data; clustered, conditional, or in-hull anomalies are not separately evaluated here. And necessity is not shown: Proposition 2 needs only an off-hull floor on the reference score, so other locality constraints could serve as the anchor; whether they do equally well is untested.

sections.heading: 8. Conclusion
sections.text: We identified a convergence collapse in fixed-target anomaly detectors: training the neural map toward its target erases the residual signal off the data, so better optimization makes the detector worse. The cause is a missing locality constraint, and we supplied it twice. kcm , the kernel-regression analog of the fixed-target family, is a closed-form, training-free detector that cannot collapse and matches the strongest trained detectors on ADBench. kar carries the same constraint into a trainable detector, regularizing a neural map to a tube around the kernel-weighted average; it is collapse-proof by construction, holds its accuracy across all 47 47 ADBench datasets and three backbones under prolonged training, and improves on the kernel anchor where the data are collapse-prone. Both rest on one principle: an anomaly detector must not be free to extrapolate its on-data behaviour past the data, and anchoring the prediction to a local kernel estimate enforces that, in closed form or as a regularizer. Accuracy under prolonged training, not at an early peak, is the right metric: the same backbone can swing by 0.1 0.1 AUROC with the stopping epoch, and a paper that quotes only the peak is reporting a regularizer it has not named. And kcm raises the bar a trained detector must clear: where a closed-form kernel smoother matches the best neural detector, the deep methods are paying their training cost for no accuracy gain. A family of tabular anomaly detectors trains a neural map toward a fixed target under squared-error loss and scores anomalies by the test-time residual; contraction matching, one-step rectified flow, and reconstruction autoencoders all fit this template. We characterize a convergence collapse : better optimization makes the detector worse. At convergence, the learned map tracks the target even off-distribution, so the residual signal vanishes on anomalies as well as on normal data. These detectors therefore rely on implicit non-convergence (early stopping, capacity caps) to retain signal. We argue this is structural: effective anomaly detection requires a locality constraint that blocks unconstrained extrapolation. Classical detectors ( k k NN, KDE, isolation forests, LOF) enforce locality explicitly; fixed-target neural detectors do not. We formalize the connection by showing that the kernel-regression analog of a fixed-target detector is a finite-bandwidth Nadaraya–Watson smoother, which we call Kernel Contraction Matching (KCM). KCM is closed-form, training-free, and CPU-efficient, yet matches established neural baselines on ADBench. Building on this bridge, we introduce the Kernel-Anchored Regularizer (KAR), which penalizes deviation of the neural prediction from a kernel-weighted average of training targets. Across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three backbones, KAR mitigates collapse and improves AUROC under prolonged training. Tabular anomaly detection identifies records that depart from normal behaviour, a long-standing problem with stakes in fraud screening, intrusion detection, condition monitoring, and medical diagnosis ( Han et al., 2022 ; Bouman et al., 2024 ) . A growing number of detectors share one design, the fixed-target template: a neural network is trained on normal data to map every input to a predetermined target , a value set in advance as a function of the input alone, and a test point is scored by its residual , the distance between the network’s output and that target. The reconstruction autoencoder uses the input itself as its target ( Sattarov et al., 2025 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ) ; flow-matching detectors instead regress a velocity field ( Li et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025a ) , with contraction matching aiming that velocity at a fixed point. Fitting a fixed target is ordinary squared-error regression, with no adversarial game, no density model, and no anomaly labels; the score is the residual, read off in one forward pass. This approach carries an implicit promise. Trained by regression, the detector should only get sharper with more epochs and a lower training loss, so training to convergence looks like good practice. We find the opposite. As the squared-error loss is minimized, detection quality first improves and then degrades. The failure is intrinsic to this class of methods, and we call it convergence collapse . At the optimum the network reproduces the fixed target on the normal data; because the target is a fixed function and the network is free to extrapolate, it reproduces the target off the normal distribution too, exactly where anomalies lie. The residual then shrinks on anomalies just as it shrinks on normal points, and AUROC declines even as the loss keeps falling. The collapsed detector is not mistrained: it has correctly solved its squared-error problem, and that problem was not detection. The pattern is not specific to one backbone: it has been studied for reconstruction autoencoders, where an expressive network reconstructs anomalies as accurately as normal points ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Ghafourian et al., 2025 ) , and we show the same failure across contraction matching and flow matching. Figure 1 shows an autoencoder, a contraction matching detector (TCCM ( Li et al., 2025a ) ), and a flow-matching detector (REFLECT ( Beizaee et al., 2025 ) ), each climbing to an early peak and then decaying toward convergence. The published strength of fixed-target detectors therefore rests on implicit non-convergence : early stopping and capacity caps that are tuned, rarely reported, and increasingly automated without naming the failure they prevent ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . The root cause is a missing constraint. The squared-error loss constrains the network only on the training data, so its score at a test point can be set by free extrapolation rather than by the nearby training points. The methods that dominate tabular benchmarks ( Han et al., 2022 ; Bouman et al., 2024 ) , among them k k -nearest-neighbour distance, the local outlier factor ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , kernel density estimation, one-class SVM ( Schölkopf et al., 1999 ) , and isolation forest ( Liu et al., 2008 ) , rest on the opposite discipline: the score at a point is set mostly by training points in a bounded neighbourhood of it. We call this property locality . Classical detectors enforce it by construction; a fixed-target neural detector, left to converge, does not. Convergence collapse is the absence of a locality constraint. Locality also points to a cure. 1 1 1 Code, configurations, and run logs: https://github.com/jose-melo/kernel-contraction-matching . Consider the kernel-regression analog of a fixed-target detector, the smoother a wide network approaches in its lazy training regime ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) . For the contraction target we call this analog Kernel Contraction Matching ( kcm ): instead of learning a map, it predicts a kernel-weighted average of the training targets, in which each training point’s influence decays smoothly with distance. kcm has no optimizer and no epoch axis, and runs on a CPU. Even so, on ADBench it matches established neural baselines ( Han et al., 2022 ; Ruff et al., 2018 ) , in line with the finding that non-deep methods are hard to beat on tabular data ( Grinsztajn et al., 2022 ) . And kcm cannot collapse: every training point’s influence is local, so its prediction levels off as a test point leaves the data and the residual grows on far anomalies instead of vanishing. kcm shows a collapse-proof solution exists, but does not let a practitioner keep a neural backbone, so we turn it into a regularizer. The Kernel-Anchored Regularizer ( kar ) penalizes the deviation of the neural prediction from the kcm prediction across the input domain, confining the network to a narrow tube around the collapse-immune kcm solution. The tube width is the only knob, expressed directly in the units of the data, so there is no loss weight to tune. Within the tube the anomaly score stays close to the kcm score at every input, AUROC can move only slightly, and the collapsed constant solution falls outside the hypothesis class. Across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three backbones, kar mitigates collapse and improves AUROC under prolonged training. The division of labour between the two is plain: kcm is the detector to deploy when scoring is the whole task; kar is for when a trainable backbone is a requirement rather than a choice , because the pipeline fine-tunes the map downstream, needs a differentiable score, or must expose a learned representation. kar ’s benchmark-wide contribution is the removal of the collapse at no accuracy cost against its anchor, not an accuracy gain over kcm . We make three contributions: (1) Convergence collapse: we show that fixed-target detectors degrade as they converge, because the network matches its target off the normal distribution and the residual vanishes on anomalies; the guarantee is formal for backbones whose training covers the off-data region and empirical for the clean-input ones (§ 3.2 ). We give a taxonomy of anomaly detectors by their off-data score behaviour. (2) Kernel Contraction Matching: we identify the kernel analog of any fixed-target detector as a closed-form, training-free, collapse-immune smoother that still matches established neural baselines on ADBench. (3) Kernel-Anchored Regularizer: we anchor a neural backbone to kcm and show this removes the collapse across all 47 47 ADBench datasets and three backbones at no accuracy cost against the anchor; on the collapse-prone subset it also improves on it. 2. Related Work Anomaly detection spans a long line of method families ( Chandola et al., 2009 ) , and its deep-learning branch is by now broad ( Pang et al., 2021 ) . Most deep detectors for tabular data learn a model of normal data and score a test point by how poorly that model accounts for it: reconstruction autoencoders by the reconstruction error ( Sattarov et al., 2025 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ) , one-class networks such as Deep SVDD by the distance to a compact centre ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) , self-supervised detectors by the consistency of a pretext prediction ( Shenkar and Wolf, 2022 ; Qiu et al., 2021 ; Yin et al., 2024 ; Thimonier et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) . A more recent line scores the residual of a generative model: diffusion-based detectors read off a denoising signal ( Livernoche et al., 2024 ; Dai et al., 2025 ) , and flow-matching detectors regress a velocity field toward a fixed target, first for images ( Li et al., 2025b ; Beizaee et al., 2025 ) and then, through contraction matching, for tabular data ( Li et al., 2025a ) . All fit the fixed-target template, and we study a failure shared by the whole template rather than adding another detector to it. Classical detectors predate these deep models and remain strong baselines on tabular benchmarks ( Han et al., 2022 ; Goldstein and Uchida, 2016 ; Bouman et al., 2024 ) . Neighbourhood methods score a point from its proximity to nearby training samples: the k k -nearest-neighbour distance ( Ramaswamy et al., 2000 ) , the local outlier factor ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , and kernel density estimation ( Lang et al., 2022 ) . One-class SVMs separate the data from the origin with a kernel of bounded reach ( Schölkopf et al., 1999 ) ; isolation forests ( Liu et al., 2008 ) and the copula-based COPOD ( Li et al., 2020 ) rank a point by how extreme it is relative to the training sample as a whole. In each design the score is read from the stored training data rather than from a parametric map free to extrapolate; LUNAR ( Goodge et al., 2022 ) folds the same neighbourhood structure back into a graph neural network. That a deep detector can be harmed by additional training is already documented, along two strands. The first concerns contamination: when the unlabelled training data contains outliers, a discriminative network fits the inliers before the outliers ( Wang et al., 2019 ) , so detection peaks early and falls as the outliers are absorbed ( Nkashama et al., 2025 ) , prompting label-free stopping criteria such as EntropyStop ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and GradStop ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) alongside evaluation protocols for unstable runs ( Perini et al., 2025 ) . The second concerns reconstruction autoencoders trained on clean normal data: a sufficiently expressive autoencoder reconstructs some anomalies as accurately as normal points ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Ghafourian et al., 2025 ) , met by autoencoder-specific responses such as a memory module ( Gong et al., 2019 ) or a penalty on the latent norm ( Ghafourian et al., 2025 ) . A third failure is mode collapse in Deep SVDD, averted by architectural restrictions on bias and activations ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) or, when those restrictions prove limiting, by explicit regularizers ( Chong et al., 2020 ) . We show the effect is a property of the entire fixed-target template, following from a single missing ingredient, locality, which also yields the cure. Our treatment of that failure draws on the link between wide networks and kernel regression: in the lazy training regime the network behaves like a fixed kernel predictor governed by the neural tangent kernel ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) , a picture normally used to study generalization, and recently to build kernel predictors for tabular models directly ( Miftachov et al., 2026 ) . We use it in the opposite direction, asking which kernel smoother a fixed-target detector corresponds to, and find that this smoother retains the locality the trained network loses. Kernel density estimation already turns a kernel smoother into an anomaly score ( Lang et al., 2022 ) ; our construction applies the same principle to the contraction target rather than to the data density. 3.
